title: Seed and stone split open
hookLine: Allah splits the grain and the date-stone, brings the living from the dead (6:95)
last: THE STARS — LOVE WHAT DOESN'T SET.

lines: A DATE PIT, HARD AS A PEBBLE.
cards: Pick up a date pit after you've eaten the fruit. It's hard as a pebble, dry, with a little groove down one side. Keep it in a drawer for a year and it would look exactly the same: finished, dead even.

Yet bury it in warm, wet soil, wait, and one day that stone cracks from the inside and a green shoot pushes out. Nobody pried it open. Surah six, verse ninety-five, points straight at that moment and says who did.

teach.h: HABB AND NAWA — GRAIN AND STONE.
teach.b: The verse says Allah is the one who splits the grain and the date-stone. Two Arabic words carry it. Habb: a grain, a seed, the kind you'd scatter for planting.
Nawa: the hard pit inside a date.

teach.h: FALAQA — TO SPLIT OPEN, LIKE DAWN.
teach.b: The verb is falaqa, to split, to cleave open, and its root names the daybreak too.
The very next verse calls Allah faliq al-isbah, the one who splits open the dawn, and the second-to-last surah of the Qur'an, al-Falaq, takes its name from the same root.
Seed and morning: two things that open from inside, on time.
Then the verse goes further: He brings the living out of the dead, and the dead out of the living.

Commentators gave many examples: the green plant out of the dry seed, and the seed out of the plant again; the chick out of the egg; and, some said, a believer born to people who didn't believe, and the reverse.
The verse ends with a question: such is Allah, so how are you turned away? It's an argument made with things you can hold. And the Prophet ﷺ cared about planting.
A hadith in Bukhari says that when someone plants a tree and a bird, a person or an animal eats from it, it counts as charity for the planter.
A report in the Musnad of Ahmad says that even if the Hour is coming and you have a palm shoot in your hand, plant it.
A seed is a small act of trust. You can't make it split. You only put it where it can.

how: Muslims read 6:95–99 as signs in agriculture and the sky; planting trees is widely encouraged as ongoing charity, following hadith in Bukhari and the Musnad of Ahmad.

o: splitting open, like a seed or the breaking dawn
a farmer's plowing of the ground before planting
the hard stone at the center of a date fruit

games.q: inside the verse — tap the pairs.
p: the hard stone of a date
the one who splits open the dawn

s: the root of split also names the daybreak
the next verse calls Allah the one who splits the dawn, and surah al-Falaq shares the root.
a hadith says planting a tree can count as charity
whatever a bird, person or animal eats from it (Bukhari).
the verse says seeds sprout by their own power alone
it names Allah as the one who splits the grain and the stone.

games.q: the Hour is arriving, and you're holding a palm shoot. what does the report in Ahmad's Musnad say to do?
games.why: plant it, if you can. the act is worth doing even when you'll never see the tree.

practice: Hold a seed, a pit, a bean or a grain of rice in your palm, or picture one, and feel how hard it is, how finished it looks. Then breathe, and imagine it underground in the dark, and the slow moment when it cracks open.

wordCard.voice: Falaq, splitting: the same root as the dawn breaking open. Allah splits the grain and the date-stone, and the dawn, and brings the living from the dead. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: the splitter of the grain and the date-stone (6:95).

carryVoice: Your line: the seed splits. You plant; the splitting isn't yours. Day four hundred one, done.

sources.ref: Musnad Ahmad 12902; al-Bukhari, al-Adab al-Mufrad 479 (plant the palm shoot)
